text.p: Howard Rollins, who shot to fame in the film "Ragtime" and earned a best supporting actor Oscar nomination for that picture, is dead. A spokeswoman for Rollins' agent said the 46-year-old actor died Sunday in New York at Roosevelt Hospital of a bacterial infection due to complications from lymphoma. Rollins was best known to television audiences for his role in the series "In the Heat of the Night." But his character was written out of the show because of Rollins' drug use. Carroll O'Connor, who worked with Rollins in the series, issued a statement saying he was "deeply saddened" by news of his death.

Country singer Faron Young is in critical condition after an apparent suicide attempt. Young, whose best known song is the melancholy ballad "Hello Walls," was being treated yesterday for an apparently self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head. The 64-year-old singer was discovered by a friend and band member in Nashville. Police say Young left a note but they did not disclose its contents. A neighbour said Young had been depressed over his emphysema anbd recent prostate surgery.

NBC has reached a settlement with Richard Jewell, heading off the libel suit the former security guard was planning to file over reports by the network linking him to the Olympic bombing. Sources say NBC has agreed to pay Jewell an undisclosed amount, but will not issue an apology. After investigating him for months, the Justice Department recently announced that Jewell had nothing to do with the crime. Meanwhile, the case of Food Lion vs ABC TV is about to begin. Opening statements are scheduled today in Greensboro, North Carolina, for the trial of the grocery chain's lawsuit against the network. Four years ago, ABC's "PrimeTime Live" aired a report charging that Food Lion sold out-of-date food.

Hollywood apparently has drawn the line at $20 million. In order to show some fiscal responsibility and stop runaway costs, there is a movement not to pay stars anything above that figure. Jim Carrey was the first to get a $20 million payday for "The Cable Guy" and Tom Cruise, Sylvester Stallone, Arnold Schwarzenegger, Mel Gibson and Harrison Ford have followed. No studio wants to be the first to break $20 million barrier but it could happen if 20th Century Fox wants Bruce Willis bad enough for "Die Hard 4." He's reportedly asking for $25 million. Sources tell Variety that Schwarzenegger, Carrey and Gibson have asked for $25 million, but have been turned down.

"Independence Day" has become the third movie in history to gross more than $400 million overseas. The special effects-laden alien invasion movie was propelled to that height by a record-breaking debut in Japan this weekend. In two days on just 31 screens it earned $4.6 million in Japan, topping the previous champ "Jurassic Park" with $3.9 million.

Among the imponderable questions raised by the latest big screen version of Shakespeare's "Hamlet" is one about time. Exactly how long is the movie, anyway? Kenneth Branagh's "Hamlet" may make history as the longest U.S. or British sound film ever released. Columbia, which is distributing the picture, puts its length at 238 minutes. Daily Variety chief critic Todd McCarthy counted 242 minutes. And another Variety critic, Derek Elley, clocks it at 246 minutes. If Elley's clock is the more accurate it would mean that "Hamlet" is longer than "Cleopatra," which came in at 243 minutes and retains the distinction of the longest talkie in U.S.-U.K. history.

There's romantic trouble ahead on "Friends." Jennifer Aniston's Rachel character will be leaving her waitress job at Central Perk in order to become a buyer for Bloomingdale's. The job -- as well as a good-looking colleague for Rachel -- will be troubling for David Schwimmer's Ross. "Suddenly she has a career and is out in the real world," says "Friends" executive producer David Crane. "It creates a lot of pressure on the relationship. Certainly it's more fun when there's conflict in a relationship. There's juicier stuff to play."

Sir John Gielgud has a new honour. The 92-year-old British acting legend was made a member of the Order of Merit yesterday by Queen Elizabeth. It's an honour that is bestowed as a personal gift by the queen to people who have made exceptional contributions to the arts, science and the armed forces. Gielgud, who was knighted in 1953, has had a long and distinguished acting career stretching over 75 years.

Goldie Hawn made her first splash dancing in a bikini on "Rowan and Martin's Laugh-In" but her dancing ambitions were more classical when she was growing up. Hawn introduced ballerina Maria Tallchief at Sunday night's Kennedy Centre Honours ceremony saying the classical dancer had been her role model. Hawn didn't become a ballerina but she says there's something of Tallchief in everything she does.

Karolyn Grimes was six years old when she played Zuzu, the little girl who believed in angels in the Christmas classic "It's a Wonderful Life." She says she'd never be part of a sequel for fear it would taint the original. "The whole movie is George Bailey and George Bailey is Jimmy Stewart," she says. "You cannot change that, so why try?" Still, Grimes can appreciate a good parody, even the "Beavis and Butt-head" episode in which an angel tries to convince Butt-head that he should kill himself by showing how the world would have been better without him. "I thought the one with Beavis and Butt-head was real cuckoo," Grimes says. "I think it's funnier than anything."
